cards.text: Jesus has just asked the Pharisees a question they can't answer, and from that day on nobody dares question Him anymore (Matthew 22:46). Now He turns to the crowds and His disciples and talks about the scribes and Pharisees, the teachers of the law and the religious leaders. He starts by saying they sit in Moses' seat.

cards.question: Since the scribes and Pharisees sit in Moses' seat, Jesus tells the crowds to ignore everything they teach.

cards.text: So practice what they tell you, BUT here comes the catch, friend. Follow the recipe card, just don't copy the baker.

cards.question: Why does Jesus tell the crowds not to do what the scribes and Pharisees do?

answers.text: They do not practice what they preach
They copy the customs of foreigners
They change the law every single year

cards.text: Then Jesus paints a picture: they tie up heavy, burdensome loads and lay them on people's shoulders. I know that feeling, friend, because back in the junk drawer every new stack of paper landed right on my head.

cards.question: The scribes and Pharisees lay heavy loads on people's shoulders. How much do they help move them?

answers.text: They will not lift a finger
They carry half of the load
They help only on feast days

cards.question: Jesus says all the deeds of the scribes and Pharisees are done for ___ to see.

cards.text: They broaden their phylacteries and lengthen their tassels. And I get wanting to be seen, friend, because in that junk drawer I'd have stretched my mustache clear out the crack if it meant somebody would SEE me.
Then Jesus starts listing what they love, and friend, the list keeps going.

cards.question: At banquets, which places do the scribes and Pharisees love?
Jesus says the scribes and Pharisees love being greeted in the marketplaces.

cards.text: They also love the chief seats in the synagogues and being addressed by the title Rabbi. Me, I'd have taken any title back in the junk drawer, where for years I was just "the thing under the takeout menus."
Then Jesus talks about that title. He says you are not to be called Rabbi.

cards.question: Why does Jesus tell His listeners they are not to be called Rabbi?

answers.text: They have one Teacher and are all brothers
The title belongs only to the priests
They have not studied long enough yet

cards.question: Jesus says not to call anyone on earth your father, because you have one ___, who is in heaven.
Jesus tells His listeners not to be called instructors either. Who does He say is their one Instructor?

cards.text: Then Jesus says who the greatest among them shall be. Lean in, friend, this one's good.

cards.question: According to Jesus, who shall be the greatest among His listeners?

answers.text: The one who is your servant
The one with the best seat
The one who teaches the most

cards.question: Whoever exalts himself will be ___, and whoever humbles himself will be ___.

cards.text: And we'll pull this batch out of the oven right there. But trust me, friend, Jesus is NOT done teaching yet.

findings.problem: Card 11 has already asked about verse 7 (the greetings in the marketplaces). Card 12 then goes back to verse 6 to tell the chief seats in the synagogues. The walkthrough steps backward here instead of moving forward through the passage. The synagogue seats should be told before the verse 7 question, or folded into card 9 or card 10's setup.

rule.text: Every story card moves the baker forward through the passage.

findings.problem: The joke doesn't share the core action of verse 4. In the verse, someone ties heavy loads onto others and won't lift a finger to help. In the joke, paper lands on Papa Dorin's head. Nobody places it there and nobody refuses to help, so the comparison misses the point of the picture.

rule.text: The everyday comparison must have the same action.

findings.problem: All three jokes in the stop (cards 5, 8 and 12) use the same setup: 'I know that feeling / I get it / Me, I'd have…' followed by a junk-drawer memory. The repetition makes the humor formulaic. Other lines read as pleasant rather than funny: card 9 ('the list keeps going') and card 17 ('Lean in, friend, this one's good'). The stop has no laugh-out-loud moment.

rule.text: No formula. His personality fits whatever moment he's in, whether it's a tense moment in a story, a hard teaching or a quick question. There are no joke quotas and no required kinds of jokes. But he is FUNNY. Not mildly amusing. Laugh-out-loud funny, the kind a baker repeats to a friend. … If a line reads like a nice dad being pleasant, push it further.

findings.problem: The wrong answer 'Master' can be argued as right, because Scripture says 'you also have a Master in heaven' (Colossians 4:1; Ephesians 6:9). 'Judge' is also arguable for a God who is in heaven. On top of that, the question says 'call anyone on earth your father' right before the blank, which hands the baker the answer.

rule.text: No near-matches. A wrong answer never means the same as the right answer, or close to it. If a baker could argue it's right, replace it.

findings.problem: Of the 11 choice cards, multiple choice has 6, fill in the blank has 3 and true or false has 2. Multiple choice dominates the stop by a wide margin.

rule.text: No formula. Which question type comes next, the order the types come in and where a blank falls are chosen naturally for each card. They never follow a pattern. No stop repeats another stop's pattern, and no type dominates a stop by a wide margin.

findings.problem: The closing line copies the example's wording ('Trust me, friend'). The rule asks for a new line each time.

rule.text: The examples show the idea. Write your own line each time.

findings.problem: The last story card is only the 'story isn't over' line and tells nothing from Matthew 23:12, but it cites Matthew 23:12.
findings.question: When the last story card is only the 'story isn't over' line and tells no verse, what should its "verses" field cite: the last verse of the passage, or something else?
